rows.en: Some of the external books that we have mentioned, and some that we have not mentioned, were creations of thoughts that issued from the fancies of the soul. And although their authors were Jews, and they were written in Hebrew and on holy soil, they were nevertheless not to the liking of the sages. Therefore the sages strove to put a check on their spread. But one must complain that as it went with the bad, so it went with the good: as they put away the former, so they put away the latter, and one fate befell them all. Indeed, from ancient days they had laid a prohibition on writing words of Torah beyond the twenty-four holy writings. In the course of time the prohibition grew lax in their hands, and they wrote various books, as we have seen until now. Aramaic translations, too, existed a long time before the destruction of the Temple (Zunz, G. d. V. [*Die gottesdienstlichen Vorträge der Juden*], p. 62), and until about the last quarter of the century before the destruction we do not find that the sages took any action to uphold and maintain the first prohibition; rather, they shut their eyes to the matter. But in the time of Rabban Gamaliel the Elder the matter changed. For then, time after time, men arose who were led by the fancies of thought, who boasted of a spirit of prophecy and made themselves Messiah. In the distress of those times most of the people believed in them, for it is easy for the soul to believe a thing that its heart desires, and it neither seeks nor inquires. At that time there also came about a renewal of religious sects, and various writings were found in the hands of their leaders; these are the ones known to us by the name 'books of the minim.' These books were dangerous to the teaching of the Pharisees, and therefore they were then compelled to warn against writing words of Torah outside the twenty-four books, and to strive to remove the external books or to store them away. Rabban Gamaliel the Elder was the first who girded up his strength to restore the prohibition to its former state and to remove from the land the books that were found. Once he was standing on top of a step on the Temple Mount, and they brought before him a book of Job in translation, and he commanded the builder, and they sank it under the course of stones (Shabbat 115a; Soferim ch. 5). From this it appears that Rabban Gamaliel commanded that all the writings be gathered in order to store them away. And when it is said there: 'they brought before him a book of Job in translation,' it implies that it was brought at his command, when he wished to store away all the writings. Perhaps it was also about his time that it was said that the gilyonim and the books of the minim are to be burned, they and the divine names in them, and storing them away is not enough, for they cast enmity, rivalry and dissension between Israel and their Father in heaven (Yerushalmi Shabbat ch. 16, and the Bavli there, and Tosefta ch. 11). This enactment reached its completion in the assembly of the sages that took place in the house of Ḥananiah ben Hezekiah ben Garon, where they deliberated on the writing of books and with great difficulty permitted the writing of Megillat Ta'anit. Then they sought to store away the book of Ezekiel, and Ḥananiah ben Hezekiah saved it from their hands (Shabbat 14b)⚠1; and according to some they sought to store away the book of Ecclesiastes (ibid. 30b), and the Song of Songs and Proverbs (Avot de-Rabbi Natan ch. 1). And as for what is said, that the Men of the Great Assembly sought to store away these two books, this is nothing but an exchange of one assembly for another: in truth the matter was disputed in a great assembly, but not in the well-known Great Assembly; rather, in the great assembly in the days of Ḥananiah. At that time they decided that Ben Sira and all the books written from then on do not defile the hands (Tosefta Yadayim ch. 2). For the decree of the defilement of the hands by the holy writings was an ancient decree (Graetz 561). And on that day they decreed — according to some — another decree concerning the holy writings: that they disqualify the terumah, and that hands that were defiled by a book also disqualify terumah (Shabbat 14a; Ḥagigah 24b). The decision that Ben Sira and all the books written from then on do not defile teaches us that all the books that defile were held by them to have been written before Ben Sira.{v1_11_16:1} But not only against the external books [did they act]; it appears that they also raised their hand to store away the translations. And as Rabban Gamaliel stored away the translation of Job, so they stored away other translations. The two translations that we have, the translation of the Torah ascribed to Onkelos and the translation of the Prophets ascribed to Jonathan ben Uzziel, were without doubt founded on ancient sources (Zunz). And if the aggadah says that the translation of the Torah was a halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai, was forgotten, and Onkelos came back and founded it, and that Jonathan received the translation of the Prophets from the prophets Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, from this we can judge that their root was very old, and therefore the views that shine forth from within them are the views of the Pharisees in an early time. Did not two sages among the greatest of the Pharisees, R. Eliezer and R. Joshua, approve the translation of Onkelos, and of the translation of Jonathan they said that secrets of the Torah were revealed in it? And even if we grant that the translations as they are before us were arranged at a late time (Geiger), nevertheless one cannot deny that their foundation already existed in writing before the time of Rabban Gamaliel the Elder, and Rabban Gamaliel stored them away. We should not wonder at their survival after they were stored away, just as we do not wonder at the survival of the book of Ben Sira and the other external books, which survived although they abolished and removed them. It is very likely that some copies of old translations remained in the hands of individuals and were saved from being stored away. Later, perhaps in the days of R. Eliezer and R. Joshua, the Targum Onkelos came to light, and the approval of great sages like R. Eliezer and R. Joshua was enough to argue in its favor and to give it endurance and survival, although it had been among the stored-away books. Likewise, when the masters of the Talmud bring an aggadah that exaggerates the great trembling with which the whole world trembled and shook on the day the translation of Jonathan was revealed, and a heavenly voice was heard saying, 'Who has revealed My secrets to the sons of men?', and Jonathan answers that he did not do it for his own honor but for the honor of Heaven, so that disputes would not multiply in Israel (Megillah 3a), the trembling and the heavenly voice are directed only against its coming to light. The meaning is: since the early sages wished to hide it, it is not right to reveal it. Thus we have seen a broad literature whose birthplace is the Holy Land, and it will teach us to know the value of the midrashim of aggadah in the books of the Oral Torah and their date, and to understand the state of the beliefs and opinions among the Jews until the destruction of the Temple.

1.note: The story of Ḥananiah ben Hezekiah and the book of Ezekiel is in Shabbat 13b; kept as printed.

rows.en: The source of the beliefs and opinions in this literature is in the holy writings, which are the foundation also of the beliefs and opinions in the literature of the Oral Torah. But it cannot be denied that opinions from foreign sources also came into its midst, and in the course of time became as if they had burst forth from the womb of our mother, the Congregation of Israel. Here we mean especially the opinions of the Greek wisdom of the Jews in Alexandria. There they occupied themselves with Greek wisdom, and with its help they devised a new way in the midrash of the Torah. In general they were faithful in their covenant with the Torah on the side of faith, and with Greek wisdom on the side of scientific knowledge, and they thought that both together are the absolute truths. Therefore, out of their desire to hold on to both together, they brought them into agreement and gave Greek wisdom a support in the divine Torah of Moses, and devised a midrash of the Torah according to the foundations of that wisdom. From this two principles of midrash came forth for them, namely the way of parable and figure. By these ways they interpreted the attributes in the Torah that ascribe a body to the essence of God. Through Greek wisdom they attained spiritual concepts of His essence that do not tolerate the attributes with which God is described in Scripture according to their plain sense, and they interpreted them by way of parable and figure. Other matters of the Torah, too, they interpreted by way of parable. Already in the days of Ptolemy Philometor the Jewish philosopher Aristobulus wrote a profound commentary on the Torah according to the philosophical opinions of his time and land, and handed it to the king to show him the glory of the Torah and its wisdom; and he testified before him that Plato knew of the Torah of Moses and that it served him as eyes in his inquiries, and that many words of the Torah had been translated for the Greeks already before the time of Alexander. And although his testimonies do not accord with the truth, at any rate it follows for us that the purpose of his commentary was to bring about agreement between the Torah and Greek wisdom, and this he achieved through their way of midrash, parable and figure. For some of them this way became a stumbling block, for through it they grew slack in practice, thinking that the statutes of the Torah are only hints to intellectual matters and that actual practice is secondary; and therefore they were not careful about keeping the practice. But the enlightened ones found fault with this and said that one must be careful in both: in the understanding of the hidden and in the keeping of the revealed (Philo, *On Abraham* 401). Philo the Jew compared the speech of the Torah to a body, and it is in our hands to give it life in several ways (ibid.). The ways in which the Torah is interpreted are two: either according to its plain sense or according to the hidden intention; and the midrash by way of parable and figure is the hidden intention. The sages in the Land of Israel did not close their hearts to this way of midrash, since from ancient days their belief was that the Torah is interpreted in several aspects, and they too spoke of secrets of the Torah. Ben Sira already hinted (ch. 39) that there is a hidden intention in the words of the Torah, and their midrashim on the Chariot were of this kind, and Ben Sira hinted at them too (ch. 49). Likewise, the effort to remove corporeality was great among the Jews from of old, and it grew still greater from the time they became acquainted with the Greeks. Was not the Septuagint made with the approval of the sages of the Land of Israel, and it already set itself this effort as its aim? And so too the Aramaic translations, whose root is ancient, as we saw above. Now we do not say that they learned these ways of midrash only from the Jews who were drawn after Greek wisdom; but we do say that these ways gained strength in the Land of Israel from the time that the Alexandrian ways of midrash became known to them. Great proof of this is found in the words of Avtalyon, who spoke of the evil that comes to religion through sages who incur the penalty of exile to another land, because the disciples who come after them will drink there the bad waters, which are the corrupt opinions (Avot ch. 1). There is no doubt that he had in mind the exile in which many sages went into exile to Alexandria and learned there from their ways and opinions. We see from this that the Land of Israel was not shut and closed before the opinions of their brothers in Alexandria. At times there is a wonderful likeness between the ways of midrash of the Alexandrians and the midrash of the sages of the Land of Israel; in particular, there are in the books of Philo many midrashim that were current in the Land of Israel (R. Zacharias Frankel, in the book on the midrashim of the Alexandrians, §§ 9, 34). The way of parable was for the sages of the Land of Israel a rule that they used in their interpretation of the commandments of the Torah,{v1_11_18:1} and especially in the narrative part and in the words of the Prophets and the Writings;{v1_11_18:2} and likewise they were accustomed, like the Alexandrians, to give reasons for the commandments.{v1_11_18:3} Josephus too, in his *Antiquities*, shows reasons of the Torah; yet Josephus was one of the Pharisees, as he himself testified. And when he speaks of the statutes and ordinances (*Antiquities*, book 4, ch. 5)⚠1 he says that he will not turn right or left from anything that Moses left us in his Torah, so that the members of his people will not complain against him if they read his words and find a deviation from the commandments of Moses. Now since we find that he gives reasons for the commandments, it is proved from this that he was sure that he would not be blamed for it, and certainly all the sages in the Land of Israel in his time went in this way. We find, further, a great likeness between the midrashim of Philo and the midrashim of the sages of the Land of Israel. When Philo sets out the narratives of the Torah, he invents rhetorical dialogues between the persons of the narratives and puts words in their mouths, as he imagined in his soul that the persons of the story ought to speak with one another, although Scripture has no hint of this. The sages of the Land of Israel did the same. Josephus did so in his narratives of the histories of the Patriarchs and the tribes, and especially the history of Moses. He puts words in the mouth of Moses when he stands before Pharaoh, and before the congregation on the day of assembly, and when he contends with the congregation of Koraḥ, and when the people murmur against him, and before his death — all of which are inventions, and there is no hint of them in Scripture. And such is the custom of the sages of the Oral Torah in their midrashim, who composed dialogues between the Holy One, blessed be He, and the Congregation of Israel, or between Him and a particular man, or between the angels and men, or between one man and his fellow, to present the matter in a fine and acceptable way. This custom gave birth to various books, such as the Book of Enoch, Fourth Ezra, Jubilees and the like. We cannot say today with whom this custom had its source, for all the writers of the nations from ancient days did so; but since the Greek writers clung to this custom with great strength, and the Jewish writers in Alexandria, disciples of the Greeks, planted it on holy soil in the interpretation of the Torah, it is very likely that the custom of the Alexandrians exerted force on them and on their midrashim. This way was useful on the one hand, for great benefit came from it in engraving moral lessons in the heart of one who reads the matters in the garment of a story; but harm for generations also came from it, for people who did not understand the matter thought that those stories were truly events that happened, and so aggadot spread about things that never were and never were created. But in the use of the way of parable and figure there is a difference between the Alexandrians and the sages of the Land of Israel. The Alexandrians went astray at the hand of Greek wisdom: they sought every philosophical opinion in Scripture and forced the verses into agreement, and therefore they twisted the pleasant words of Scripture and found in every simple story hints to intellectual matters, and interpreted the names of the persons of the stories as having special meanings. And events that our faith holds to have actually happened, they subtilize and interpret as some opinion in the sciences and in the influence of reason, and they say that the story is a parable and figure. Philo too did so in his midrashim. He explained (in the book *On Noah* 192) that the Garden of Eden is a parable for the garden of wisdom and contemplation, which teaches man knowledge of his soul and its powers. And he says (in the book *On the Confusion of Tongues* 302) that the story of the generation of the dispersion is a figure of the causes that move and bring about the confusion of opinions and the debasement of virtues. The names of Abraham and Sarah he interprets by way of figure: Abraham is the figure of the depth of reason, and Sarah the figure of righteousness, which is a princess [sarati] among the virtues (in the book *On Abraham* II, 15). Not so did the sages of the Land of Israel go astray. If they interpret Scripture by way of figure, their intention is mostly only to express words of praise and glory about the deeds of the righteous, or disgrace and reproach⚠2 about the deeds of the wicked, in the language and style of Scripture; but they never thought that this was truly the intention of the verse. And even where their intention is to interpret by way of figure, and they found in the verse a hint to some matter, there is never a contradiction between the outer side of the story or saying that is interpreted and its inner side, which is the hint and the figure; nor is it found that they would say of an event that happened according to the plain sense of Scripture that it is only a parable. And if they said that what Moses threw into the water at Marah was not wood of a growing kind but a parable for words of Torah, by their way this is no contradiction of the plain sense, for in their view 'tree' is said also of words of Torah. From the great multitude of midrashim that were expounded by way of parable and figure, and in giving reasons for the words of the Torah, it appears that these ways were greatly honored among the sages; and already in an early time they gave special names to those who went in these ways of midrash: those who interpret by way of parable and figure were called dorshei reshumot (Mekhilta Va-Yassa ch. 1, and in many places), and those who interpret by way of giving a reason for the Torah were called dorshei ḥamurot (Ḥullin 134b; Pesaḥim 54a, and in many places). And they said of the interpreter of the first kind that he interprets 'as a kind of parable' (Mekhilta Mishpatim ch. 6), and of the interpreter of the second kind that he interprets 'as a kind of ḥomer' (Kiddushin 22b; Sotah 15a). Now, after we have understood a little of the character of the midrashic literature that grew up in the Land of Israel, and after we have further seen the relation of the midrash of the Alexandrians to the midrash of the sages of the Oral Torah, and how far the former poured of its spirit upon the latter, it will not be hard for us now to bring forth from the remnants of that literature, together with the midrashim of aggadah in the books of the Oral Torah, the opinions of the Jews until the destruction of the Temple and the foundations in the beliefs and principles of the Jewish religion.

1.note: Josephus's statement that he has added nothing to what Moses left is in Antiquities 4.8.4 (§§196–197); kept as printed.

2.note: Printed ותהלה ('praise'); the sense requires a word of blame (perhaps תפלה or קללה). Rendered by sense as 'reproach'.

rows.en: Beliefs and Opinions of the Jews.

The foundations of the beliefs and opinions on which the Jewish religion is built are the Torah and the other holy writings. Of the manner in which these foundations were understood, and how they lived within the nation from the day they came up from the exile until the destruction of the Temple, nothing complete and ordered has reached us; but from the midrashic remnants in the books of the Oral Torah and the other books of the Jews of that time we shall recognize well the opinions of the Pharisaic Jews and come to know the cornerstones of their beliefs, which were sealed with the seal of the early time.

The attributes of God's essence in the holy writings are mostly corporeal attributes. But it was already hinted in the Torah itself that these attributes are not to be taken in their plain sense. When it is said: 'for you saw no manner of form' [Deuteronomy 4:15], or: 'for man shall not see Me and live' [Exodus 33:20], or 'Is the Lord's hand shortened?' [Numbers 11:23], this was a compelling proof for one who reflects that the essence of God has no form, and that the concept of seeing God and the attribute 'the hand of the Lord' are nowhere to be understood according to their literal meaning. It is true that in the most ancient times they did not enter into subtle inquiries on the essence of God, and did not attend to the consequences that follow from believing in the existence of God in this way or that. But from the time that enlightenment increased, and especially from the time that the opinions of the sages of the nations among whom they dwelt became known to them, and they grew accustomed to inquiries into metaphysical matters, it was impossible that this should not be for them a great stimulus to reflect in speculative inquiry on the lofty cornerstone of the attributes with which the essence of God is described in Scripture. In the Septuagint we already find the effort of the sages of Israel to soften⚠1 the attributes of corporeality. And although that translation is not the work of the sages of the Land of Israel, at any rate it was made with their approval. And the Aramaic translations, whose root is ancient, made this effort their cornerstone. Some of the emendations of the Scribes also show their desire to remove corporeality, as was already explained above. And a Jewish sage of Alexandria — Aristobulus — said to Ptolemy Philometor: 'As in common speech we use the word "hand" to signify power ... so it is in the words of the Torah' (Eusebius, *P[raeparatio] E[vangelica]* VIII, 10). In these words we find, almost word for word, a saying current in the mouth of the sages of the Land of Israel: 'The Torah spoke in the language of men.' And although this saying is found only regarding the interpretation of doubled expressions in the Torah, nevertheless the example in the words of Aristobulus shows us that it was said also about the attributes of corporeality. And in different words this saying is found explicitly on this matter: 'We describe Him so as to soothe the ear with what it is able to hear; we describe Him by His creatures' (Mekhilta Ba-Ḥodesh ch. 4). It is clear that the sages of the Land of Israel strove to remove corporeality (R. Ḥayyim Oppenheim in my journal *Beit ha-Midrash*, p. 65). But they did not enter into philosophical speculations like the Alexandrians; they went in their simplicity, and with the help of their midrash on the Torah they interpreted and decided. One idea runs through all the midrashim of the sages: that the essence of God is simple, is not a body, and is exalted above the thought of man; and because He is simple they also called Him by abstract names and called Him 'Might' (Gevurah) and 'Shekhinah.' But God reveals Himself to men according to the measure of their human apprehension, and the vision that they see is not so in essence; rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, shows it to them so by way of miracle. And since, according to their belief, God reveals Himself to men in a corporeal vision, therefore it is permitted also to speak of Him in corporeal attributes. This idea goes round through all the midrashim of the sages. In the simplicity of their faith they found the source of this idea in the Torah and the Prophets, saying that the Torah's words 'This is my God and I will glorify Him' [Exodus 15:2] teach that God was revealed to Israel in a sensible vision by way of miracle, so that the maidservant at the sea saw a vision of God and pointed at Him with her finger (Mekhilta Shirah ch. 3). And it was easy for them to explain the saying 'The Lord is a man of war' [Exodus 15:3], which is corporealization with respect to God, who fills heaven and earth; for they believed that the Holy One, blessed be He, out of His love for Israel, was revealed to them in various visions: once as a man of war, in order to sanctify His name (ibid. ch. 4), and once as an old man full of mercy (ibid. and Ba-Ḥodesh ch. 5). And they said well that these modes of the revelation of the Shekhinah depend on the deeds of Israel: that they make His right hand left if they do not do His will, and His left hand right if they do His will; and He neither slumbers nor sleeps if they do His will, and, as it were, there is sleep before Him if they do not do His will. Already the addition of the words 'as it were' shows that it means to say that the action of Israel causes them to imagine a change in His actions. And one of the Tannaim who lived in the first century after the destruction said: 'At times the world and its fullness cannot contain His divinity, and at times He speaks with a man from between the hairs of his head' (Genesis Rabbah ch. 4). And another Tanna explains the Torah's words 'and when I see the blood' [Exodus 12:13], which is a corporeal attribute, and interprets that the meaning is that as the reward for a commandment that Israel performs, the Holy One, blessed be He, reveals Himself and has pity on them (Mekhilta Bo ch. 7). We have no clearer effort to remove corporeality than their saying that if it is written in the Torah 'a jealous God' [Exodus 20:5], the intention is not to describe God with the attribute of jealousy, for jealousy does not rule over Him, but He rules over jealousy (ibid. Ba-Ḥodesh ch. 6). There is no counting such traces in the books of the Oral Torah. Thus we have seen that their belief in the essence of God was not in a corporeal manner. And if their words about God are corporeal words, this is no proof about their concepts and their belief, for so it was of old and so it will be forever, that men speak of God in human attributes. But although their apprehension of the essence of God was spiritual, nevertheless they did not enter into philosophical speculations and did not interpret according to scientific premises and abstract inquiries; rather, they took their premises only from the holy writings, and in relation to Scripture they interpreted this cornerstone, and even this only by a slight hint.

footnotes.en: The explanation of the words 'from then on' is: from the writing of Ben Sira on. R. Ẓevi Graetz, in his commentary on the book of Ecclesiastes, in the appendices at the end of the book, p. 166, explains 'from then on' as from the assembly in the house of Ḥananiah ben Hezekiah, or from the day on which R. Eleazar ben Azariah was appointed Nasi, when they also spoke about certain books with regard to the defilement of the hands (Yadayim 3:5). He relies on the Yerushalmi, Sanhedrin 10:1: 'R. Akiva says: Also one who reads in the external books has no share in the world to come, such as the books of the minim; but the book of Ben Sira and the book of Ben La'anah and the books of Homer and all the books written from then on, one who reads in them is like one who reads a letter.' His intention is that here 'from then on' necessarily does not refer to the writing of the books, for these three kinds of books were not written at one time; therefore 'from then on' must refer to the time of the assembly. But I cannot decide, for he brings us a reading in the Yerushalmi that I did not find there; the reading before us is: 'has no share in the world to come, such as the book of Ben Sira and the book of Ben La'anah; but the books of Homer and all the books written from then on ...', and according to this reading 'from then on' refers to the writing of the books of Homer. That scholar strove there to prove that the book of Ecclesiastes was written at the end of the days of Herod, and that in the upper chamber of Ḥananiah ben Hezekiah the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel disputed whether to attach it to the holy writings and whether it defiles the hands, and the matter was not settled until the day on which they seated R. Eleazar ben Azariah in the academy. I must apologize for not heeding his decision, for there is much to question in his proofs, and especially regarding several readings that are not found in our books. There is no room here to go on at length, but I will bring the main reason that moved me to depart from his decision: namely, that I found that Hillel quoted a verse from the book of Ecclesiastes (Tosefta Berakhot end of ch. 1). Thus in the days of Hillel it was already held to be one of the holy writings. And even before Hillel, Simeon ben Shetaḥ quoted (Yerushalmi Berakhot 7:2, and in many places) two verses from the book of Ecclesiastes: 'In the shadow of wisdom, in the shadow of money,' and 'the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom gives life to those who have it' [Ecclesiastes 7:12]. Therefore what they disputed, whether Ecclesiastes defiles the hands, does not mean whether to attach it to the holy writings, for it had long been among the Writings; rather, they wished to store it away, as they wished to store away the book of Ezekiel.

As: 'and they shall spread the garment' [Deuteronomy 22:17] — this is a parable (Mekhilta Mishpatim ch. 6, 13); R. Ishmael interpreted three things by way of parable. 'Nor put a stumbling block before the blind' [Leviticus 19:14] — before one who is blind in a matter (Sifra Kedoshim ch. 2). 'And honor the face of the old man' [Leviticus 19:32] — this is one who has acquired wisdom (Kiddushin 32b); and the Targum⚠1 of 'you shall rise up before the hoary head' [Leviticus 19:32] is 'before one who is learned in the Torah,' and its parallel is in the book of the Wisdom of Solomon (14:8–9)⚠2. 'A just hin' [Leviticus 19:36] — that your yes be just and your no be just (Bava Metzia 49a). 'Do not profane your daughter to make her a harlot' [Leviticus 19:29] — this is one who marries his daughter to an old man (Sanhedrin 47a)⚠3. 'You shall not eat with the blood' [Leviticus 19:26] is interpreted for several matters by way of parable (Sanhedrin 63a); and likewise 'you shall not plant for yourself an Asherah' [Deuteronomy 16:21], 'you shall not remove your neighbor's landmark' [Deuteronomy 19:14], and many more like these.

footnotes.en: 'And behold, a vine was before me' [Genesis 40:9] — this is the Torah (Ḥullin 92a). 'And the Lord showed him a tree' [Exodus 15:25] — He showed him words of Torah, which are compared to a tree (Mekhilta Va-Yassa ch. 1). 'Go forth and behold, O daughters of Zion, King Solomon' [Song of Songs 3:11] — the children who are distinguished, the King to whom peace belongs (end of Ta'anit; Sifra; Seder Olam). There is no need to go on at length with examples, for all the books of the Oral Torah are full of this kind. The Song of Songs is interpreted entirely by way of parable, and they said of it that it is the most excellent of songs and is holy of holies.

The days of consecration are called 'a sweet savor' because the Holy One, blessed be He, acquired a friend for Himself and makes a festive day for Him (Sifra Tzav). 'Lest the land fall into harlotry' [Leviticus 19:29] — because he has intercourse with many women, etc. (Tosefta Kiddushin ch. 1). Why did He put the taking of the Passover lamb first, etc. (Mekhilta Bo ch. 5). 'Both man and beast' [Exodus 12:12] — the one who was first in transgression, with him the punishment begins (ibid. ch. 7; Sotah 9a). 'Bring before Me the omer so that the grain may be blessed, and the two loaves so that the fruits of the tree may be blessed' (Tosefta Rosh Hashanah ch. 1; Sukkah ch. 3; and the Gemara, Rosh Hashanah 16a). Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai loved to give reasons for the commandments (see Tosefta Bava Kamma ch. 7, and Mekhilta Mishpatim ch. 12; Bava Kamma 79b; Kiddushin 22b, and the Yerushalmi there). 'Why did the Torah warn concerning the stranger,⚠1 etc.' (Bava Metzia 59b). The meal-offering of the sotah is of barley, because her deed was the deed of a beast, etc. (Sotah 14a); and see further there (8b). Some translators were accustomed to give reasons for the commandments in their translations (Yerushalmi Berakhot 5:3). In a later time it was the manner of several sages to expound the reasons of Scripture (Kiddushin 65b⚠2, and in many places). In several places in this work of ours we have noted that this was the custom of our ancients. See *Me'or Einayim* ch. 6, which brings several reasons of Scripture given by the masters of midrash that agree with the interpretations of Philo.
